transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

What brings me in is… I’m having a really hard time keeping my mind on one thing long enough to actually finish it. And it’s not just boring stuff, or things I don’t care about—it happens even when it matters.

I work in computer support, so I’ll be trying to trace a client’s network problem, going through logs or checking connections, and then ten minutes later I’ll realize I’ve been staring at the same entries over and over. Like I’ve reread the same lines three times and still couldn’t tell you what they say. I’m physically sitting there doing the task, but my mind just… doesn’t stay with it. And then I lose the thread of what I was investigating and have to start over, which is frustrating and honestly kind of embarrassing.
When did you first start noticing these difficulties with staying focused? Was this something you experienced even as a child, or did it begin more recently as an adult?

It definitely goes way back. I mean, I notice it more now because work has real consequences and everything is more complicated, but it’s not new.

My mother still brings it up—she kind of jokes about it, but it’s one of those jokes that has a lot of truth in it. She says my grade school report cards were always some version of, “He’s bright, but…” You know, “doesn’t stay in his seat,” “blurts out answers,” “misplaces assignments.” And the homework thing was especially frustrating because sometimes I actually had done it, but then I’d lose it before turning it in, or it would be stuffed in the wrong folder or left somewhere. So it wasn’t like I just didn’t care or couldn’t understand the work.

I don’t know if people took it that seriously back then. It was more treated like I was just careless or needed to try harder. But looking back, yeah, the focus and sitting-still kind of problems were there when I was a kid.
As a child, were you also unusually active or impulsive—like fidgeting a lot, having trouble staying seated, or acting without thinking?

Yes, that was definitely part of it. My mother still jokes about it, actually—she’ll say, “Your report cards all basically said the same thing: bright kid, but…” And then it would be things like I didn’t stay in my seat, or I’d blurt out answers before the teacher finished asking, or I’d lose homework even when I’d actually done it.

The homework one still kind of bothers me to think about, because it made me look irresponsible, but sometimes I really had completed it. I’d just manage to misplace it or leave it somewhere or have it in the wrong place when it was time to hand it in. But yes, the being out of my seat and speaking before thinking—that was something people commented on pretty early.
Have you continued to experience symptoms like restlessness, difficulty staying seated, or acting impulsively in your adult life, or have these mostly been limited to your childhood?

No, it definitely didn’t stop in childhood. It’s still there now, just… it looks a little different because I’m not a kid in a classroom anymore.

Even when I’m supposed to just sit still and listen—like in a meeting, or when someone is explaining something at work—I get this feeling like there’s a motor humming under my skin. That’s the best way I can describe it. I may be sitting there, but internally it feels like I need to get up, check something, fix something, move to the next problem right that second. It’s not just boredom, exactly. It’s more like this pressure in my body to do something.

And I try to control it, because obviously I’m an adult and I know I can’t just keep jumping up or interrupting people. But it takes effort. Sometimes I’m sitting there thinking more about how hard I’m trying to stay put than about what the person is actually saying. It’s embarrassing, honestly, because from the outside maybe I look impatient or like I don’t care, but inside it feels like I’m fighting this constant urge to move or act.
Outside of work, do you find these issues with focus and restlessness also affect other parts of your life—like at home, in social situations, or when trying to relax?

Yes, absolutely. It’s not just a work thing. Honestly, sometimes it’s even more obvious at home because the things that are supposed to be relaxing are the things I seem to have the hardest time doing.

Like, if I try to read something quiet—say a manual for something around the house, or instructions for a device—I’ll start with good intentions, and after a few minutes I’m rereading the same paragraph, then making some little comment under my breath, then checking my phone, then getting up to “just do one thing” that doesn’t really need doing. And by the time I come back, I’ve lost the thread completely.

Movies are another one. My wife can sit and watch a whole movie like a normal person, and I’ll want to, I really will, but after a bit I start shifting around, muttering comments, looking something up on my phone, getting up to get water or adjust something or whatever. Sometimes there isn’t even a real reason—I just feel like I can’t keep sitting there quietly.

And I’ve tried those breathing exercises, because people say they’re supposed to calm you down, but I usually make it maybe a few minutes before I’m irritated or distracted or thinking, “How long has it been?” Then I’ll check the time or abandon it. It’s frustrating because these are supposed to be simple, peaceful things, and somehow they feel like work.
Do you ever find yourself feeling down or losing interest in things you used to enjoy, even for long stretches of time?

I’m not really sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean, I have days where I feel frustrated or worn out, and I can get pretty discouraged with myself, especially when I feel like I’m not keeping up with things the way I should. But if you mean feeling down in a way that lasts for weeks and weeks, or losing interest in everything I normally enjoy… I don’t know that I’d describe it that way.

I still do want to do things, at least in theory. Sometimes I don’t follow through well, or I bounce away from them, but that feels different from not caring about them, if that makes sense. Like I might plan to watch something, read something, or work on something, and then I don’t stick with it—but I wouldn’t say it’s because I’ve lost all interest or feel emotionally flat about it.

So… no, I haven’t really noticed long stretches like that. Not in the way I think you’re asking.
Can you think of times when you’ve had trouble focusing or felt restless in situations that aren’t work-related—like when you're at home with family, out with friends, or running errands?

Yes—honestly, days off are probably the clearest example. I’ll tell myself, “Okay, today I’m going to rest. I’m not going to turn this into a project day.” And then somehow by nine in the morning I’ve already taken apart a laptop I meant to just look at for five minutes.

Then while I’m doing that, I’ll notice something else—like the garage shelves are messy—so I’ll go out there “just to check” where a tool is, and next thing I know I’m half-rearranging a shelf. But I don’t finish that either, because I’ll remember I owe someone a move in an email chess game, so I go back inside, open the laptop, then while I’m there I notice cables piled up under the desk and start reorganizing those.

It’s this constant bouncing around. It’s not like I’m choosing one thing and steadily working through it. It’s more like I keep getting pulled into the next thing that catches my attention. And by the end of the day, I’ve been busy the entire time—I mean, really busy—but nothing is actually fully done. The laptop is still open, the garage looks worse because I moved things around, the cables are half-sorted, and I’m tired but also annoyed because I never really rested either.
